tldr: By reformulating robot end-effector constraints using analytic inverse kinematics (IK), this work constructs lower-dimensional spaces that satisfy constraints by definition and vectorizes both IK and collision checking via CPU SIMD instructions, speeding up constrained motion planning by up to 10x (down to microseconds to milliseconds).
hero_caption: A 23-DOF bimanual mobile manipulator (RB-Y1) executes a whole-body pick-and-place task planned by the proposed method, lifting a box from the floor with both hands and carrying it to a desk. It achieves millisecond-level real-time motion planning while strictly maintaining a rigid geometric constraint on the relative pose between both hands as well as whole-body center-of-mass stability.
overview:
When a robot carries a cup of water without spilling or transports a large box with both hands, it requires constrained motion planning (CMP) to strictly maintain the end-effector orientation or relative pose. However, the set of robot joint angles that satisfy these constraints (the constraint manifold) forms a surface with zero volume (a measure-zero subset) within the full search space. As a result, standard sampling-based planners that generate and connect random configurations struggle to produce valid solutions on the constraint manifold, leading to prohibitive computation times.

Recently, methods like McVAMP have achieved major speedups by utilizing CPU SIMD instructions to repeatedly push (project) joint-space samples back onto the constraint manifold. However, iterative numerical projection has a weak spot: the number of steps required to converge varies per input, leaving parallel lanes idling while waiting for the slowest sample. This paper turns its attention to an alternative approach: space reparameterization through analytic inverse kinematics (IK) that solves end-effector constraints directly in closed form. Planning in a lower-dimensional space, such as the end-effector pose, ensures constraints are satisfied by construction. Furthermore, because analytic IK runs in fixed computational steps without loops, it maps exceptionally well to SIMD vector parallelism.

The authors built "ReVAMP", a system that systematically eliminates conditional branches such as if-statements from analytic IK, allowing multiple intermediate configurations to undergo IK resolution and collision checking in parallel. In experiments, they evaluated the method on a 7-DOF arm navigating a planar maze, a 14-DOF bimanual setup for cooperative manipulation, and a 20-DOF mobile manipulator performing whole-body pick-and-place. The results demonstrate up to a 10x speedup (reaching microsecond to millisecond scales) over state-of-the-art projection-based methods. Because planning becomes so fast, the authors also show that complex sequential manipulation pipelines can be redesigned into much simpler structures.
contributions: Pre-compiled evaluation of the analytic IK-based reparameterized space into branchless instruction sequences, enabling ultra-fast evaluation via CPU SIMD vector operations.

Introduced an early rejection filter that checks end-effector geometry for collisions before computing full-body IK, leveraging the fact that the sampling space is parameterized directly around end-effector poses.

Achieved up to a 10x speedup over state-of-the-art methods (such as McVAMP) across constrained robotic systems ranging from 7 to 20 DOFs, demonstrating millisecond-level replanning and strict constraint satisfaction on a physical robot.

Showed that sub-millisecond planning speeds allow replacing heuristic-heavy grasp and placement candidate selection with a simple brute-force approach that plans between all candidate pairs to pick the shortest path.

sections.heading: Breaking through the constrained motion planning barrier with vectorization and reparameterization
sections.summary: Constrained motion planning for tasks like bimanual carrying or maintaining level end-effectors is notoriously difficult because the valid solution space has measure zero. While recent SIMD-accelerated projection planners (McVAMP) are fast, they suffer from inefficiencies caused by waiting for iterative projections to converge. This paper resolves that bottleneck by uniting analytic IK reparameterization with vector operations.
sections.details:
When robots perform practical tasks in the real world, they frequently must operate while maintaining geometric constraints on their end-effectors. For example, when a bimanual robot carries a cardboard box with both hands, the relative pose between the two end-effectors must stay fixed throughout the motion so the box is neither dropped nor crushed. In the full joint configuration space (C-space), the region satisfying such constraints shrinks into a volume-less, razor-thin subset (a constraint manifold). Consequently, standard sampling-based motion planners that sample random configurations and connect paths struggle to draw valid constraint-satisfying samples at all.

To tackle this challenge, recent works (VAMP and McVAMP) leveraged CPU SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) vector instructions to parallelize robot forward kinematics, collision checking, and numerical projection that pushes configurations back onto the constraint manifold, driving planning times down into the microsecond-to-millisecond regime. However, the numerical projection approach has an inherent weakness. Because it relies on iterative solvers like Newton's method, the number of convergence steps varies from sample to sample, causing parallel processing lanes to stall while waiting for the slowest sample. In experiments on a 7-DOF arm, 16% of the projection time was spent merely waiting for the final sample in a vector batch to converge.

The authors instead revisit an alternative formulation: reparameterization. When end-effector constraints can be expressed analytically, one can define a lower-dimensional parameter space incorporating the constraints (such as 3D end-effector position plus redundant angles) and invert joint angles via analytic IK. Searching within this space guarantees that all generated configurations satisfy the geometric constraints from the start. Historically, analytic IK-based methods were bottlenecked by calling IK functions hundreds or thousands of times during edge validation. However, analytic IK evaluates through fixed algebraic expressions without loops, making it an ideal candidate for SIMD vector parallelism. This study proposes "ReVAMP", a new framework that pre-compiles and vectorizes analytic IK to achieve real-time motion planning even for high-dimensional systems.

sections.heading: Optimization, projection, learning... Where does vectorized IK stand?
sections.summary: Constrained motion planning encompasses optimization-based, sampling-based projection, learning-based, and analytic IK-based approaches, along with hardware acceleration via GPUs and CPU SIMD. This work pushes the analytic IK-based dimensionality reduction approach to its limits using fine-grained CPU SIMD parallelism.
sections.details:
Research in constrained motion planning (CMP) broadly falls into four categories.

The first comprises optimization-based methods (such as TrajOpt and cuRobo). These treat constraints as soft penalty terms in an objective function. However, they may produce slight constraint violations or get trapped in local minima, missing global paths.

The second consists of sampling-based motion planners (SBMP) paired with numerical projection or numerical continuation. They project random configurations onto the measure-zero manifold using the Jacobian pseudoinverse. While offering reliable global exploration, projection is computationally expensive and only satisfies constraints within a tolerance ($\\epsilon$), which can be problematic for high-precision tasks.

The third encompasses recent learning-based methods. These learn constraint manifolds within neural network latent spaces, but collecting training data and retraining whenever constraints change presents practical hurdles.

The fourth, serving as the direct inspiration for this work, is reparameterization via analytic IK. Using tools like IKFast, these methods solve analytic IK to map directly from a lower-dimensional end-effector space to joint space, satisfying constraints identically. However, existing implementations struggled with wall-clock speed due to the overhead of calling heavy IK functions repeatedly during edge validation.

From a parallelization standpoint, efforts include multi-seed optimization on GPUs (e.g., cuRobo) and fine-grained CPU SIMD parallelization for collision checking and numerical projection (e.g., VAMP/McVAMP). This paper overcomes the stalling issue McVAMP suffered during iterative projection by utilizing the non-iterative nature of analytic IK in SIMD, redefining the performance ceiling of reparameterization approaches.

sections.heading: Formulating end-effector constraints and mapping them to lower-dimensional spaces
sections.summary: This section outlines the mathematical definitions of C-space, task constraints, and the constraint manifold $M$. It explains the theoretical basis for mapping end-effector poses and self-motion parameters to unique joint configurations via analytic IK, reformulating $M$ into a lower-dimensional parameter space $\\mathbb{P}$ with positive measure.
sections.details:
Let the robot joint configuration space (C-space) be $C\\subset\\mathbb{R}^d$, with the obstacle-free subset denoted as $C_{\\text{free}}$. The robot end-effector (EE) pose is given by the forward kinematics mapping $\\text{FK}: C\\to SE(3)$.

Constrained motion planning (CMP) requires satisfying task-defined constraint functions $F(q)=0$ where $F: C\\to\\mathbb{R}^k$. This defines the constraint manifold $M=\\{\\,q\\in C\\mid F(q)=0\\,\\}$, through which the robot must find a collision-free path in $M_{\\text{free}}$ from start to goal. Most end-effector constraints are expressed on the EE pose as $g(\\text{FK}(q))=0$, including requirements like keeping a cup upright or locking the relative transform between two arms.

Conversely, inverse kinematics (IK) computes joint angles $q$ from an EE pose $X$, but the solution is generally not unique. For kinematically redundant robots, specifying discrete solution branches $b$ alongside continuous self-motion parameters (redundancy angles $\\psi\\in\\Psi$) yields a unique function $q = \\text{IK}_b(X, \\psi)$. Using this property, a reparameterization of $M$ is defined as a pair consisting of a parameter space $\\mathbb{P}$ and a continuous mapping $\\Phi: \\mathbb{P}\\to C$ such that $\\Phi(\\mathbb{P})\\subseteq M$.

Here lies the key insight: while $M_{\\text{free}}$ has measure zero in the original C-space, the valid region $P_{\\text{free}}=\\{\\,p\\in\\mathbb{P}\\mid\\Phi(p)\\in C_{\\text{free}}\\}\\$ possesses positive measure (non-zero volume) within the reparameterized space $\\mathbb{P}$. Consequently, uniform sampling within $\\mathbb{P}$ naturally yields samples that satisfy the constraints 100% of the time by construction. In this way, constrained motion planning is mathematically converted into an unconstrained planning problem in a lower-dimensional parameter space.

sections.heading: Eliminating branches entirely to solve IK simultaneously via SIMD
sections.summary: The authors propose stripping all if-statements and conditional branches from analytic IK and pre-compiling the routines for targeted hardware. Converting data structures to SoA allows calculating IK for multiple poses in parallel using SIMD, which, combined with end-effector-only early collision filtering, drastically accelerates edge validation in sampling-based planners.
sections.details:
The core of this method lies in transforming analytic IK and parameter mappings into branchless instruction sequences that CPU SIMD registers can execute in parallel, embedding them directly into edge validation within a planner (Alg. 1).

### IV-A Reparameterization Generation via Pre-compiled Analytic IK
Standard C++ code generated by tools like IKFast contains numerous if-statements for inverse trigonometric range checks and singularity handling, hindering SIMD parallelization. The authors apply a two-step transformation. First, discrete self-motion manifold (SMM) branches (up to 16 configurations determined by shoulder, elbow, and wrist signs) are separated into compile-time static templates rather than runtime branches. Second, data-dependent branches, such as domain clamping for inverse trigonometry and angle wrap-around, are reformulated into smooth saturation losses instead of hard branches. If all loss values are negative, the IK solution is valid; if any value is positive, the configuration violates joint limits or singularities and is deemed invalid. Using a tracing compiler built on Pinocchio and CppAD, inverse trigonometric functions are polynomial-approximated, generating optimized machine-code instruction sequences completely free of loops and branches.

### IV-B Vectorization of Trace-Compiled Computations
With branches eradicated, data memory layouts can be repacked from traditional Array of Structures (AoS) to Structure of Arrays (SoA). This allows AVX instructions on modern CPUs (which compute eight 32-bit floats simultaneously on 256-bit registers) to feed the identical IK instruction sequence across 8 parameter inputs within shared clock cycles, recovering 8 joint configuration vectors at once.

### IV-C Accelerating Constrained Planning in Parameterized Spaces
In sampling-based planners like RRT, most compute time is spent on edge validation, which interpolates between nodes and checks for collisions (Alg. 1). In ReVAMP, multiple waypoints interpolated in parameter space $\\mathbb{P}$ are converted to joint space simultaneously using vectorized IK, evaluating joint limits and reachability in parallel. The resulting states are passed to VAMP's vectorized broad-phase and narrow-phase collision checkers. If even one waypoint is invalid, the entire edge is immediately rejected (early retirement).

Two clever design choices further boost efficiency. The first is early end-effector collision filtering. In manipulation, the end-effector (EE) sweeps through the largest volume and is most prone to collisions. Because the sampling space directly contains the EE pose, the planner checks EE collisions first without needing forward kinematics (FK) or joint-space conversions. This skips over 90% of unnecessary IK evaluations. The second is a joint continuity check: if any joint jumps by more than 0.15 rad between consecutive waypoints, the edge is rejected, preventing the robot from crossing kinematic singularities and ensuring smooth path execution.

Ghosted arm silhouettes show intermediate configurations explored during planning, while the green line marks the solution path traced by the end-effector. Parameterizing the EE pose directly enables highly efficient early collision filtering against maze walls.

sections.heading: Evaluated from 7 to 20 DOFs: 10x speedup and pipeline simplification
sections.summary: The authors evaluated performance on a 7-DOF arm in a planar maze, a 14-DOF bimanual arm in cooperative carrying, and a 20-DOF whole-body mobile manipulator in box pick-and-place. ReVAMP runs up to 10x faster than state-of-the-art McVAMP, maintains strict constraint compliance on hardware (0.2 mm error), and simplifies complex sequential manipulation pipelines.
sections.details:
Experiments were run primarily on an Intel Core i7-13700K (5.4 GHz), progressively increasing degrees of freedom and constraint difficulty.

### V-A 7-DOF FR3 under Task-Space Planar Constraints
The task requires the end-effector to stay flush with the floor with roll and pitch locked while escaping a maze. The parameter space is effectively $SE(2)\\times\\Psi$ (4 dimensions). Across 200 maze scenarios, ReVAMP was compared against the state-of-the-art projection-based McVAMP. ReVAMP showed superior scaling in planning times. In particular, it identified unsolvable problems (failure cutoff times) 10x faster than McVAMP. Thanks to deterministic IK calculations without iterations, the planner quickly discards invalid paths. An ablation on early EE collision filtering revealed that 91.6% of invalid edges were dismissed purely from EE collisions before computing IK, dramatically cutting wasted computation. On real hardware powered by a low-spec CPU (Core i5-6500T) (Fig. 5), the arm replanned around dynamic obstacles while keeping end-effector deviations down to an average of just 0.2 mm (arising purely from low-level tracking error), confirming strict constraint adherence.

### V-B 14-DOF Bimanual Iiwa under Cooperative Manipulation Constraints
This benchmark evaluated carrying an object with both hands under a fixed relative transform. Two parameterizations were tested (both 8-dimensional): a Leader-Follower setup (sampling one arm's pose and solving the other via IK) and a Dual-Follower setup (sampling the object's pose and solving both arms via IK). Compared to McVAMP, computation time per iteration was substantially lower. In the Leader-Follower formulation, overall planning was 6x faster despite requiring 5x more iterations. The Dual-Follower formulation exhibited even higher search efficiency, showing that a well-chosen parameterization can also sharply reduce iteration counts.

### V-C 20-DOF RB-Y1 Whole-Body Pick-and-Place
Using a 20-DOF system (6-DOF torso + two 7-DOF arms, with the base stationary), the robot solved whole-body pick-and-place to lift a box from the floor onto a table. With an additional inequality constraint for center-of-mass (CoM) stability (keeping the CoM within the support polygon), the valid region covered merely 0.012% of the parameter space. While existing pipelines (IFT) prune grasp, transit, and placement candidates using heuristics, ReVAMP's extreme speed allowed restructuring the pipeline: it solves constrained motion plans across all candidate triples via brute force and picks the shortest one. Even though the number of motion planning queries jumped 10x, overall planning time dropped by roughly 20x, speeding up end-to-end pipeline execution by 2.5x on average.

captions.F5: Experimental setup for dynamic maze navigation using the physical FR3 robot. Even when a person places blocking obstacles directly in the maze corridors or the arm's workspace, the robot replans instantly on a low-power PC, reaching the goal while keeping the end-effector pressed tightly against the maze floor with an average deviation of only 0.2 mm.

sections.heading: Conclusions and outlook: Shifting planning paradigms toward faster TAMP
sections.summary: By pre-compiling robot kinematic structures into analytic IK and vectorizing them via SIMD, ReVAMP speeds up constrained motion planning by up to 10x. Future directions include expanding beyond single-branch limits and applying the method to task and motion planning (TAMP).
sections.details:
This paper introduced ReVAMP, which leverages robot kinematic structure to pre-compile analytic IK and rapidly evaluate constraint-satisfying parameter spaces using CPU SIMD instructions. By eliminating iterative convergence overhead and processing through deterministic computation, it achieved up to a 10x speedup over numerical projection methods across 7-to-20-DOF constrained planning problems. This speed makes motion planning no longer the primary pipeline bottleneck, opening up opportunities to simplify high-level task design.

One current limitation is that planned trajectories must remain within a single self-motion manifold (SMM) branch. Unlike numerical projection, which can drift across branches, fixing the analytic IK branch prevents the robot from crossing kinematic singularities to flip its elbow configuration within a single query. While the authors note that many practical tasks are fully solvable within a single branch, extending the method to support transitions across multiple branches remains an open challenge. Automating the branch-elimination process from raw IK code is another area for future work.

Looking ahead, the authors envision pre-compiling kinematic derivatives (Jacobians) to automate optimal grasp selection. Furthermore, in an environment where motion planning is nearly computationally free, they anticipate fundamentally restructuring sampling strategies within Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) to tighter harmonize symbolic reasoning with geometric planning.

takeaways: Analytic IK can be pre-compiled into branchless instruction sequences, unlocking massive CPU SIMD vector parallelism (such as solving 8 poses in a single instruction sequence).

Parameterizing the search space around end-effector poses allows collision checking the end-effector first without computing forward kinematics, skipping over 90% of invalid IK evaluations and detailed link checks early.

Unlike iterative numerical projection, analytic IK runs in fixed computational steps, allowing invalid edges to fail instantly (10x faster failure detection) and preventing stalled parallel execution.

Achieving sub-millisecond constrained planning allows abandoning complex candidate-filtering heuristics in favor of brute-force planning across all candidate combinations, yielding simpler and more optimal manipulation pipelines.
limitations: Paths are restricted to a single self-motion manifold (SMM) branch, meaning a single planning query cannot generate motions that pass through singularities to flip elbow or wrist configurations.

While highly effective for end-effector constraints with closed-form solutions (translational, rotational, or bimanual constraints), it cannot be directly applied to arbitrary non-linear constraints, such as closed kinematic chains lacking analytic IK.
Replacing conditional branches from IKFast code with saturation losses still involves manual tuning, leaving fully automated compilation pipelines for arbitrary robot models as future work.
